title: How to Save a Relationship: 12 Steps to Rebuild Trust
h1: How to Save a Relationship: 12 Steps to Rebuild Love, Trust and Respect
description: Learn how to save a relationship that feels like it's slipping away, with 12 practical steps for honest talks, forgiveness, boundaries and reconnecting.
excerpt: If your relationship feels stuck or fragile, these 12 steps help you own your part, talk honestly, forgive and fall back into partnership.
intro:
Maybe the arguments have become constant. Maybe it is the opposite: you barely talk anymore. Or something happened, a lie, a betrayal, a long period of neglect, and now you are both wondering whether there is anything left to save. The good news is that many relationships that feel broken can be rebuilt when both people are willing to do the work.

This guide lays out 12 steps on how to save a relationship, from owning your mistakes and changing how you communicate to forgiving, setting boundaries and rediscovering why you chose each other. You will also find honest guidance on when saving it is not the healthiest choice.
body:
First, ask whether you both want to save it

A relationship can only be saved by two people. One partner working overtime while the other checks out is not repair; it is exhaustion. Before diving into the steps, have a calm conversation where you each answer: “Do I want this to work, and am I willing to change some of my own behavior to get there?” If you both say yes, even tentatively, you have something to build on.

Also check for safety. If there is ongoing abuse, control or intimidation, the steps below do not apply. More on that at the end.

Take responsibility for your part

1. Admit your mistakes, specifically

Most struggling relationships involve hurt on both sides. Start with your own. Vague apologies like “Sorry if I upset you” do little. Specific ones do a lot: “I've been dismissive when you bring up money, and I know that made you feel alone with it.” Owning your part first often makes it easier for your partner to own theirs. Our guide on how to apologize breaks down what a real apology includes.

2. Stop the behaviors that cause the most damage

Some habits are especially corrosive: contempt (eye-rolling, mockery, sarcasm meant to wound), harsh criticism of character, defensiveness and stonewalling. Relationship researcher John Gottman identified these four as strong predictors of breakups. You cannot fix everything at once, but you can commit today to dropping the insults, the silent treatment and the scorekeeping.

Change how you talk to each other

3. Communicate to understand, not to win

When a conversation gets heated, slow it down. Let your partner finish, then reflect back what you heard: “So you feel like I prioritize work over us. Is that right?” Feeling understood lowers defenses faster than any argument. Then share your side using “I feel” language instead of “you always.”

4. Schedule regular check-ins

Pick a weekly time, even 20 minutes, to talk about how things are going: what felt good this week, what was hard and one thing each of you needs. Regular check-ins stop small resentments from piling up into explosions.

Tip: If conversations keep escalating, agree on a pause signal. Either of you can call a 20-minute break when you feel flooded, as long as you both agree to come back to the topic. It prevents saying things you can't take back.

Rebuild your friendship and connection

5. Improve your friendship

Strong couples are usually good friends. They know each other's worries, dreams and daily routines. Ask questions you have not asked in a while: “What's stressing you out at work lately?” “What's something you've been wanting to try?” Curiosity is the opposite of taking someone for granted.

6. Make real time for each other

Connection needs time, and time needs a calendar. Protect a weekly date, a phone-free dinner or a Sunday walk. Doing something new together, like a class, a hike or a new recipe, can bring back some of the energy you had early on. For more ideas, read how to grow your relationship.

7. Revisit your best memories

Look through old photos, retell the story of how you met or go back to a place that mattered. Remembering the good times is not about living in the past; it reminds you both what you are fighting for.

8. Show love in their language

Your partner may feel loved through words, quality time, help with tasks, touch or thoughtful gifts. If you have been expressing love in your language and not theirs, small shifts can make a big difference. See how to show love for practical ideas.

Repair trust and set healthy boundaries

9. Respect each other's wishes

Respect means taking your partner's needs seriously even when they differ from yours: needing alone time, wanting to see family more often, asking you to check in when you are late. Respect also means not pressuring them to change their mind.

10. Set clear boundaries together

Boundaries protect the relationship. Agree on what is and is not okay, like how you handle disagreements in front of others, how much time goes to work or friends and what transparency looks like after a breach of trust. Write them down if that helps, and revisit them as things improve.

11. Forgive, and rebuild trust with action

Forgiveness is a process, not a single conversation. The person who caused harm rebuilds trust through consistent, transparent actions over time. The person who was hurt eventually chooses to stop using the past as a weapon. Neither part can be rushed, and both are necessary.

12. Respect your differences

You will never agree on everything, and you do not have to. Many couples have “perpetual problems,” long-running differences in personality or preference that never fully resolve. The goal is to talk about them with humor and understanding instead of treating each one as a crisis.

A 30-day plan to get started

Change feels more doable with a plan. Here is a simple month-long structure you can adapt together:

  • Week 1: Reset. Each of you names one behavior you will stop (for example, sarcasm or phone use at dinner) and one you will start. Have your first weekly check-in.
  • Week 2: Reconnect. Plan one date that feels like the early days and one evening with no screens. Ask each other three questions you have never asked before.
  • Week 3: Repair. Choose one recurring conflict and talk it through using the listening and pause techniques above. Aim for understanding, not a final solution.
  • Week 4: Review. Discuss what has improved, what still feels hard and what you want to keep doing. Decide together whether outside help would make the next month easier.

Small, repeated actions are what rebuild a relationship. One great conversation helps, but it is the weekly habits that change how you feel about each other. For more ongoing ideas, read how to improve your relationship with your boyfriend.

When to get professional help

If you have tried on your own and keep getting stuck in the same cycle, a licensed couples therapist can help. Therapy is especially useful after infidelity, during major life transitions or when one of you is considering leaving. Going early, while you still like each other, is more effective than waiting until you are both depleted. If your partner will not go, individual therapy can still give you clarity.

When saving it isn't the right goal

Not every relationship should be saved. Consider stepping back if:

  • Only one of you is trying, over a long period.
  • Trust keeps being broken in the same way despite promises.
  • You feel afraid, controlled or belittled.
  • You want fundamentally different futures, such as children or location, with no compromise possible.

If you are unsure, our guide on how to know when your relationship is over can help you think it through. And if you recognize signs of control or emotional abuse, read about mentally abusive relationships.

Tip: If you feel unsafe with your partner, reach out to the National Domestic Violence Hotline, available 24/7 at 1-800-799-7233, by texting START to 88788 or at thehotline.org. Leaving an abusive relationship is about safety, not failure.

The bottom line

Saving a relationship comes down to two willing people doing small, consistent things: owning mistakes, talking with respect, making time for each other, forgiving and protecting what you are building. It will not happen overnight, but many couples look back on their hardest season as the moment they learned to truly be partners.
takeaways: A relationship can only be saved if both partners are willing to change.
Start with specific apologies and drop contempt, criticism, defensiveness and stonewalling.
Weekly check-ins, protected time together and curiosity rebuild your friendship.
Get couples counseling early; and don't try to save a relationship that isn't safe.

faq.q: Can a relationship be saved after a lot of fighting?
faq.a: Often, yes, if both partners want to change how they fight. Replacing criticism and contempt with calm, specific requests, taking breaks when flooded and holding regular check-ins can transform the pattern. A couples therapist can help if you keep getting stuck in the same loop.

faq.q: How do you save a relationship when one person wants out?
faq.a: You cannot force someone to stay. You can listen to their reasons without defensiveness, own your part, ask if they are open to counseling or a set period of genuine effort, and respect their answer. If they still want to leave, focusing on your own healing is the healthiest step.

faq.q: How long does it take to rebuild trust?
faq.a: There is no fixed timeline. Rebuilding trust after a serious breach often takes many months of consistent, transparent behavior from the person who broke it, along with patience from the person who was hurt. Couples counseling can make the process clearer and more structured.

faq.q: What are signs a relationship is worth saving?
faq.a: Good signs include mutual respect beneath the conflict, both partners willing to work on it, shared core values and goals, moments of real affection and the absence of abuse. If you still like each other as people and want the same future, there is usually something to build on.
